name: A vision model looks at each font once and writes a description (neutral specimen sheets, 0-3 mood scores plus a short 'look' phrase)
what_it_is: A one-off labelling run: render every family as a neutral specimen (no font name, same text for every font), show it to a vision model, and store a short text label per family in a data file the search prompt can read. The label I tested is: four 0-3 scores (motion, futuristic, loud, calm) plus a look phrase of at most 12 words, produced from sheets of 6 fonts (rows) per PNG. A production label would use Google's own mood words as the score keys so it can be checked against Google's weighted tags, and would keep the free-text look phrase for the LLM to read.
provider_and_url: Anthropic models through the API (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5) or through claude -p on the subscription, the way server/vibe.ts already calls Claude. Vision limits and image token formula: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision . Evidence on how well vision models see type: FontBench, Reading != Seeing (arXiv 2603.08497, March 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.08497 ) and Texture or Semantics? Vision-Language Models Get Lost in Font Recognition (arXiv 2503.23768, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23768 ). My own pilot: SCRATCH/vv/render.mjs (renders sheets), SCRATCH/vv/sheets/*.png, SCRATCH/vv/blind_ratings.json, haiku_ratings.json, sonnet_ratings.json (SCRATCH is the session scratchpad from the brief).
catalog_coverage: Everything with a readable file can in principle be rendered. My renderer (fontkit outlines to PNG, no browser) was run only on the 48 pilot families. The same fontkit outlines read cleanly for 2,082 of 2,099 families in the measured-traits run: Google 1,743 of 1,760; Fontshare 64 of 64; Velvetyne 63 of 63; Collletttivo 26 of 26; Tunera 23 of 23; Use & Modify 163 of 163, so rendering should work for those; the 17 Google failures are colour or layered fonts and a few odd subsets, which a browser canvas would draw. 479 families have a real italic; an italic specimen would be a second row. Pilot coverage was small: 48 families, all Google, none from the 339 non-Google rows.
granularity: Per family at one weight (the pilot used the file nearest 400), optionally one extra row per italic. Weight and italic are poorly judged by vision models (FontBench), so they should come from measurement, not from this label.
signal_type: Overall visual look and mood impression, written by a model that sees the letters.
mood_dimensions_covered: Pilot (mine, n=48, all Google, stratified: picked to over-represent Active and Futuristic). Raters saw 8 PNG sheets, 6 fonts per sheet, text 'Hamburgefonstiv 0123' plus a pangram, black on white, no names, and scored each row 0-3 for motion (fast, action), futuristic, loud, calm. Scored against Google's family-level weighted tags (Active, Futuristic, Loud, Calm >= 50; positives among the 48: 15, 13, 6, 7). AUC / Spearman: Sonnet (subagent, blind to the tags): motion 0.89 / 0.75, futuristic 0.89 / 0.68, loud 0.98 / 0.69, calm 0.80 / 0.34. Me (Sonnet 5.5, the running agent; I rated before looking at any tag but I knew the sample was stratified for Active and Futuristic): 0.89 / 0.83, 0.90 / 0.74, 0.98 / 0.70, 0.81 / 0.35. Haiku (subagent through the Agent tool's haiku option, exact version not shown, presumably 4.5 [uncertain]; blind): 0.78 / 0.47, 0.69 / 0.42, 0.86 / 0.65, 0.50 / 0.00. Mean of the three: 0.96 / 0.82, 0.91 / 0.71, 0.97 / 0.73, 0.76 / 0.29. So motion and futuristic are well covered by a Sonnet-class model (the brief's example, 'fast movement or action', is the best case), loud is covered, calm is moderate, and Haiku is clearly worse and at chance on calm. Not tested: elegant, handmade, playful, vintage and the rest of Google's vocabulary. Script, brush, blackletter, pixel and techno looks are the kind a model sees at once; subtle moods (sincere, business) are untested.
query_style_specificity: Better for tight pictorial requests (brush, blackletter, techno, pixel, wide black display, formal script) than for loose affective words; in the pilot it was good at the two sharpest moods (motion, futuristic) and weaker at calm. Haiku compressed its scale: 44 of its 48 motion scores were 1 or 2, so it separates little.
quality_evidence: Own pilot (above), with 15, 13, 6 and 7 positives, so each AUC carries roughly +-0.05 to +-0.1 of noise. On the same 48 fonts, the measured-traits model (grouped cross-validation, see the measured-traits item) scored AUC 0.94 Active, 0.81 Futuristic, 0.99 Loud, 0.89 Calm; vision (me) 0.89, 0.90, 0.98, 0.81; the rank sum of both 0.97, 0.91, 1.00, 0.91. Measurement is as good or better on weight, slant and calm; vision is better on futuristic; combining helps most on Active and Futuristic. Agreement between raters: Sonnet and I agree at Spearman 0.79 to 0.96 across the four scores; Haiku agrees with Sonnet only at 0.32 to 0.50, so a Haiku label would be a noisy copy. Published evidence is a warning for anything beyond overall look. FontBench (arXiv 2603.08497; 26 fonts, 4-way multiple choice, random 25%): Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored 28.0% on font style (regular, bold, italic, bold-italic), 64.0% on font family, 44.8% on size, 97.6% on colour; the paper reports a 'regular' bias: models predict regular for 67-80% of all style questions whatever the truth. The Font Recognition Benchmark (arXiv 2503.23768; 15 fonts): best model about 30% on the easy version and about 15% on the hard one; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 31.3% easy and 8.4% when the text spells a font name. Both measure identifying a named font or a style label from one render, not describing the overall look, and not relative judgements across several fonts on one sheet, so they do not contradict the pilot; they do say to take weight and italic from the files.
known_noise: Model-to-model variance is large (Haiku against Sonnet 0.32-0.50 Spearman). Scores are coarse (0-3). Run-to-run variance at the same temperature was not measured [uncertain]. Position on the sheet or neighbouring fonts may bias a row's score (relative judgement helped the pilot, but I did not test row order) [uncertain]. The pilot's one clear miss: BBH Bartle, a heavy squared display face I scored futuristic 3 and Google weights 20. Vision models are known to be blind to weight and italic (FontBench), so a label that says 'bold' or 'italic' should be overruled by the measured values.
name_and_memory_bias: Real and not removed. While rating I recognised the shapes of several popular families (my scratch notes say things like 'Orbitron-ish' and 'Teko-like'), so part of my 0.89-0.90 AUC may be memory of how those families are usually described, not seeing. The sample was all Google fonts, which models know well; the 339 non-Google rows are exactly where memory cannot help, and I did not test them. Names are not shown, so the evocative-name effect is gone, but recognition from shape is not. The tag side has the same issue: Google's tags were made by people looking at the same fonts.
untagged_rows: Ranked fairly if every row is labelled: the label is generated from the picture, so a Velvetyne or Fontshare face gets the same kind of label as Roboto. This is the main attraction for the weakly tagged tail. Counts: 137 Google families have no Google tag at all, 336 have one or none, and the 339 non-Google rows carry foundry keywords or use-cases (Fontshare: Logos, Magazines, Branding) but no Google-style mood words. A label run over those 476 rows (339 + 137) is 80 sheets of 6.
text_interference_risk: Real, so the specimen must be neutral. FRB shows the Stroop effect: when the text spells a font name, models answer from the words (70.1% of their errors in the hard version were 'content-biased misattribution'; the best model fell from about 30% to about 15%). Rules I followed in the pilot: the same sample text for every font ('Hamburgefonstiv 0123' and 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog'), never the family name, never a mood word, black on white, no row labels. Do not render words like 'fast' or 'techno' in the specimen, and do not put the family name in the prompt text next to the image.
integration_path: Offline builder (for example scripts/label-looks.ts): (1) render sheets of 6 families, as in SCRATCH/vv/render.mjs (about 140 lines on fontkit, 8 sheets / 48 fonts rendered in a few seconds; colour fonts need a browser canvas instead); (2) send each sheet to a Sonnet-class model with a fixed schema: per row {look: <= 12 words describing shapes only, scores: {active, loud, calm, futuristic, playful, elegant, handmade...: 0-3 in Google's own mood words}}; (3) write server/data/looks.json = {family: {look: 'heavy slanted brush letters, rough edges', s: {active: 3, loud: 3}, model: 'claude-sonnet-5-5', v: 1}}; (4) in compactCatalog append the look phrase (about 12 words) or only the words behind scores >= 2 as extra row text. Alternative: use the 0-3 scores as numbers in a scoring step before the LLM (LLM turns the request into a weight per mood, code ranks, LLM re-ranks a shortlist). Store the model id and a prompt version in the file so a later model switch can relabel.
tokens_per_row: Look phrase of 12 words: about 16-20 tokens per row, about 35k tokens over 2,099 rows (range 31k-42k), nearly doubling the current catalog text (about 40k tokens by characters/4). Only the top mood words (scores >= 2): about 6-8 tokens per row, 13k-17k in total. Labelling only the 476 weakly tagged rows with the phrase: about 8k. All characters/4 estimates, not tokenizer counts [uncertain]. Static text, so it stays inside the cached system prompt.
vocabulary_alignment: Can be forced onto Google's vocabulary by naming Google's mood words as the score keys (what the pilot did with Active, Futuristic, Loud, Calm), which also makes the labels checkable against Google's weighted tags for the 1,613 tagged Google families. The free-text look phrase adds new words.
explainability: Good for the phrase ('heavy slanted brush letters, rough edges' can be quoted back to the user); the 0-3 scores are a model's opinion, not a measurement, and cannot be verified except by looking.
determinism: Frozen once generated, so search is as deterministic as the file. Regenerating can change labels (sampling, model updates); I did not measure run-to-run agreement [uncertain].
build_effort: About 1 agent-day: the renderer exists as a prototype (SCRATCH/vv/render.mjs), plus a batch driver with resume, the schema, a check against Google tags (python3 SCRATCH/vv/analyze5.py shows the pattern), and the compactCatalog change. Calling through claude -p needs the image reachable by the model (a file path read through its Read tool, or stream-json image input; I did not test either with claude -p [uncertain]).
per_search_cost_and_latency: Nothing at search time except a bigger cached prompt (+13k to +42k tokens depending on the label form). I could not measure the latency effect; the app's own note puts a follow-up at about 7 s with thinking off, and a larger prompt is read from cache [uncertain].
one_off_cost: API estimate, my arithmetic: image tokens = ceil(width/28) x ceil(height/28) (Anthropic vision docs); a 1400x900 sheet is 1,650 tokens (capped at 1,568 on Haiku 4.5's standard tier), a 1000x300 single-font image 396. Assumed 400 prompt tokens and 100 output tokens per font. Prices per million tokens from the claude-api model table cached 2026-09-25: Haiku 4.5 $1 / $5, Sonnet 5.5 $2 / $10, Opus 5.5 $4 / $20; batch API at 50%. Scheme A, 6 fonts per sheet, 350 sheets for 2,099 families: Haiku $1.74 ($0.87 batch), Sonnet 5.5 $3.54 ($1.77 batch), Opus 5.5 $7.07 ($3.54 batch). Scheme B, one font per image: $2.72, $5.44, $10.88 ($1.36, $2.72, $5.44 batch). Sonnet and Opus think by default; each 1,000 thinking tokens per sheet adds about $3.5 (Sonnet) or $7 (Opus), so set effort low [uncertain]. Adding the 479 italics: 430 sheets instead of 350. Through claude -p on the subscription: no dollars, but quota and time. Observed in my pilot: a Haiku subagent took 62 s and 87k tokens for 8 sheets (48 fonts) and a Sonnet one 49 s and 108k tokens, both including fixed agent overhead; scaled to the catalog that is roughly 40-50 minutes sequential [uncertain].
human_effort: About 2 hours: write and test the prompt, look at 20 rendered grids next to their labels, spot-check the weakly tagged rows. Growth: label only new families (about $0.003 each at API prices, one sheet per 6).
asset_access: Same files as the measured-traits item (Fontsource woff2 on jsDelivr, cdn.fontshare.com, and the 275 indie files already in server/.cache/fonts); the renders are made locally and nothing is scraped. Images go to Anthropic's API or claude -p; Anthropic's vision FAQ says uploaded images are not stored beyond the request and not used for training (API documentation; I did not check the subscription path).
licence_and_provenance: Specimen images are derivative renderings, not font files. Google rows are OFL (1,716), Apache (36), UFL (5) and a few others, which allow rendering and use; indie rows are mostly OFL with a few CC BY, GPL-with-exception and Bitstream Vera. Fontshare (63 rows) is under the ITF Free Font License: free personal and commercial use, no redistribution or resale of font files; a rendered image sent to an API is not a font file, but I found no ITF text on AI use [uncertain]. The labels are our own data (model output); keep the model id and prompt in the file as provenance.
etiquette: Only font files already fetched or cached; no scraping; nothing from velvetyne.fr (its Velvetyne files came from the app's cache). API use should respect rate limits; the batch endpoint is made for this. My font fetches for the pilot were 48 requests to jsDelivr.
maintenance_and_freshness: Labels go stale only when a family is redrawn or the vocabulary changes. New families need one sheet row each. Switching model or prompt means relabelling everything (about $2-4, or an hour), so record the model id and prompt version with each label. Re-run a 50-family agreement check against the previous labels before replacing them.
risks_and_limitations: (1) The pilot is small (n=48, 6-15 positives) and all Google; no indie font was tested. (2) Part of the score may be memory of famous fonts rather than perception. (3) Haiku, the model the search uses today, is the weak rater (calm at chance), so labelling must be done by a stronger model. (4) Weight and italic are not seen reliably (FontBench), so do not let the label override measurement. (5) The labels are one model's opinions, not shared with Google's vocabulary unless the keys are Google's words. (6) A stratified sample makes AUCs look better than they would be on the whole catalog. (7) Sheet position and neighbours may bias scores; I did not randomise row order [uncertain]. (8) Adding 13k-42k tokens of label text to every search prompt costs subscription quota and may dilute the rest of the catalog line.
evaluation_hook: As in the pilot, bigger: label 150-200 families that have Google tags, rate blind, and report AUC and Spearman per Google mood against the measured-traits baseline and against Haiku; add 20 rendered grids for a person to rate for indie and Fontshare rows, which have no tags to check against. Randomise row order in a second run to see position effects.
recommendation_for_font_explorer: USE PARTLY, after measured traits. Run it once with a Sonnet-class model (not Haiku), with scores keyed to Google's mood words plus a short look phrase, over the 476 weakly tagged rows first (339 non-Google + 137 untagged Google): about 80 sheets, roughly $0.8 on Sonnet 5.5 at API prices ($0.4 batch) or under 10 minutes of claude -p. Why: it is cheap, it covers the rows where tags are missing, and in the pilot it beat measured traits on Futuristic (0.89-0.90 against 0.81) while the two together were best for Active and Futuristic (0.97 and 0.91). Why not first or alone: measured traits are free, deterministic, name-free and already match it on Active, Loud and Calm; and vision labels carry untested memory bias and cannot see weight or italic. Take weight, width and slant from the files and the 'look' from the model. Smallest first step: take SCRATCH/vv/render.mjs, render sheets for the 476 rows, label them with Sonnet 5.5, compare on the Google-tagged subset against the measured-traits model, then add only the top mood words to those rows in compactCatalog (about 3.8k tokens).
